Longitudinal models: latent transitions and growth mixtures

longitudinal.Rmd
library(latentmixtures)
data(substance)
data(depression)

Latent transition analysis: substance use from grade 8 to grade 12

A latent transition analysis (LTA) has one latent class variable per wave and first-order transitions between consecutive waves (Collins and Lanza 2010). substance records past-30-day alcohol use, binge drinking, cigarette smoking and cannabis use (0/1) of 1,500 students in grades 8, 10 and 12 (alc_1, binge_1, cig_1, mj_1, alc_2, …). It was generated from three statuses (Non-use, Alcohol use, Polysubstance use) with invariant item probabilities, progression over time and attrition. Which statuses are there, and how do students move between them?

# the items of each wave, in the same order: alc_t, binge_t, cig_t, mj_t
waves <- lapply(1:3, function(t) paste0(c("alc_", "binge_", "cig_", "mj_"), t))
t3 <- substance |> lta(waves = waves, K = 3)
#> Starting Julia ...
convergence(t3)       # check that the best LL is replicated and EM reached the maximum
#> Convergence check: ✓ no problems found
#>   best start converged      yes (104 EM iterations)
#>   stage-2 starts converged  20 / 20
#>   best LL replicated        20 times
#>   LL at EM / after Newton   -6512.0856 / -6512.0856 (gain -9.1e-13; max |gradient| 2.1e-13)
#>   smallest class            0.085
#>   · EM converged; 1 Newton steps (polish = true) raised the log-likelihood by 8.5e-07 (max |gradient| 1.3e-03 → 7.6e-07); the reported solution is the Newton one
t3
#> ━━ Latent transition analysis ━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━

classprobs(t3)        # class-by-wave proportions: non-use declines from grade 8 to 12
#>            [,1]      [,2]      [,3]
#> [1,] 0.76243593 0.5408827 0.3857451
#> [2,] 0.15266639 0.3110786 0.3659523
#> [3,] 0.08489768 0.1480387 0.2483026
round(transitions(t3)[[1]], 2)   # grade 8 -> 10; rows sum to 1
#>         to
#> from     class1 class2 class3
#>   class1   0.69   0.24   0.07
#>   class2   0.10   0.73   0.17
#>   class3   0.00   0.17   0.83
itemprobs(t3, wave = 2)$cig_2
#>       class1    class2    class3
#> 0 0.98241983 0.8779346 0.4507763
#> 1 0.01758017 0.1220654 0.5492237

The generating transition matrix from grade 8 to 10 is (rows: from Non-use, Alcohol, Poly) [.70 .24 .06; .12 .68 .20; .03 .17 .80]; the estimate is close (classes are ordered by their size at wave 1).

waves lists the indicators of each wave, in the same item order: the first item of every wave is the same question, and so on. It accepts tidyselect expressions inside list() written in the call (list(alc_1:mj_1, alc_2:mj_2, alc_3:mj_3)), column positions (list(2:5, 6:9, 10:13)) or character vectors. Missing items and whole missing waves (attrition) are handled by full-information maximum likelihood.

Measurement invariance across waves

By default the item-response probabilities are equal across waves (invariance = "full"), so that a class means the same thing at every wave and transitions are interpretable. With invariance = "none" they are estimated separately at each wave. The two models have the same number of classes and are nested, so they can be compared with the scaled likelihood-ratio difference test:

t3_free <- substance |> lta(waves = waves, K = 3, invariance = "none")
compare_models(t3, t3_free)
#> ━━ Nested model comparison ━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━
#>   t3 (M0) nested in t3_free (M1)
#> 
#>   ─────────────────────────────────────
#>   Model               LL  Par.  Scaling
#>   ─────────────────────────────────────
#>   M0: t3       -6512.086    26   1.0104
#>   M1: t3_free  -6505.781    50   1.0581
#>   ─────────────────────────────────────
#> 
#> ── Difference tests ────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
#>   ──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
#>   Test                                 Chi-square  df      p
#>   ──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
#>   Likelihood ratio (naive, ML)             12.609  24  0.972
#>   Satorra-Bentler (2001) scaled (MLR)      11.362  24  0.986
#>   ──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
#>   Scaling correction of the difference cd = 1.1098
#>   ΔAIC = 35.391, ΔBIC = 162.908, ΔsaBIC = 86.667 (M1 - M0)

A non-significant scaled test (and a lower BIC for the invariant model) supports invariance, which holds in the generating model. Transitions can also be constrained to be equal over time; here they were not (more students start using alcohol between grades 10 and 12):

t3_stat <- substance |> lta(waves = waves, K = 3, transitions = "stationary")
compare_models(t3_stat, t3)
#> ━━ Nested model comparison ━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━
#>   t3_stat (M0) nested in t3 (M1)
#> 
#>   ─────────────────────────────────────
#>   Model               LL  Par.  Scaling
#>   ─────────────────────────────────────
#>   M0: t3_stat  -6514.783    20   0.9986
#>   M1: t3       -6512.086    26   1.0104
#>   ─────────────────────────────────────
#> 
#> ── Difference tests ────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
#>   ──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
#>   Test                                 Chi-square  df      p
#>   ──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
#>   Likelihood ratio (naive, ML)              5.394   6  0.494
#>   Satorra-Bentler (2001) scaled (MLR)       5.140   6  0.526
#>   ──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
#>   Scaling correction of the difference cd = 1.0494
#>   ΔAIC = 6.606, ΔBIC = 38.485, ΔsaBIC = 19.425 (M1 - M0)

For the posterior probabilities of a given wave use posterior(t3, wave = 2). Covariates, sampling weights, standard errors and continuous indicators are not yet available for LTA models in the R interface (the Julia package fits continuous LTA, e.g. for wellbeing_panel).

Growth mixture models: adolescent depressive symptoms

growth() models a repeated continuous measure, one column per wave in time order.

  • model = "lcga": latent class growth analysis (group-based trajectories, Nagin 1999): every class has its own trajectory and there is no variation around it.
  • model = "gmm": growth mixture model (Muthén and Shedden 1999): growth factors vary normally within class, with a covariance matrix that is equal across classes (the Mplus default).

depression holds depressive symptoms (CES-D-10, 0–30) of 600 adolescents at ages 12 to 16 (dep1–dep5), generated from four trajectory classes: low stable (share 0.54), increasing (0.27, a quadratic rise that levels off), decreasing (0.10) and chronic high (0.09), with random intercepts, slopes and curvature within class and attrition that depends on earlier symptoms. Which trajectories are there?

lcga4 <- depression |> growth(dep1:dep5, K = 4, model = "lcga", degree = 2)
gmm4  <- depression |> growth(dep1:dep5, K = 4, model = "gmm", degree = 2)
convergence(gmm4)     # check that the best LL is replicated and EM reached the maximum
#> Convergence check: ✓ no problems found
#>   best start converged      yes (366 EM iterations)
#>   stage-2 starts converged  20 / 20
#>   best LL replicated        20 times
#>   LL at EM / after Newton   -7168.4319 / -7168.4319 (gain 0.0e+00; max |gradient| 6.3e-08)
#>   smallest class            0.095
#>   · EM converged; 1 Newton steps (polish = true) raised the log-likelihood by 1.5e-08 (max |gradient| 4.3e-03 → 2.1e-07); the reported solution is the Newton one
growthparams(gmm4)    # alpha: factor means by class; psi; theta: residual variances
#> $alpha
#>                class1    class2     class3      class4
#> intercept  3.85176545  5.558791 13.9719810 15.15414693
#> linear     0.42367462  2.199611 -1.8708160  0.59141538
#> quadratic -0.01851456 -0.132383  0.1070532  0.02189505
#> 
#> $theta
#>     dep1     dep2     dep3     dep4     dep5 
#> 4.650693 6.399899 5.514008 5.595880 5.768606 
#> 
#> $psi
#>            intercept     linear  quadratic
#> intercept  2.9587253 -1.2328642  0.1771084
#> linear    -1.2328642  1.0486808 -0.1310774
#> quadratic  0.1771084 -0.1310774  0.0281375
lm_table(lcga4, gmm4, format = "markdown")

Model fit

Model K Par. LL AIC BIC saBIC Entropy Smallest (%)
lcga4 4 20 -7252.738 14545.477 14633.415 14569.921 0.864 10.4
gmm4 4 26 -7168.432 14388.864 14503.184 14420.641 0.795 9.5

LL = log-likelihood; Par. = free parameters; saBIC = sample-size adjusted BIC; Smallest = smallest class (estimated proportion).
Lowest information criteria in bold.

The class-specific intercepts, slopes and curvatures are close to the generating values (4, 0.3, 0), (5, 2.6, -0.25), (14, -2.0, 0.1) and (15, 0.6, 0); the GMM fits much better than the LCGA because individuals vary around their class trajectory.

By default the time scores are 0, 1, 2, ... and the trajectories linear. Use times for unequally spaced waves or another time origin, e.g. ages centred at 14, so that the intercepts are the class means at age 14:

lcga_14 <- depression |> growth(dep1:dep5, K = 4, model = "lcga", times = 12:16 - 14, degree = 2)
growthparams(lcga_14)$alpha
#>               class1     class2     class3       class4
#> intercept  4.3208622  9.1525130 10.5394274 16.282323191
#> linear     0.2827088  1.5600996 -1.3981562  0.697964593
#> quadratic -0.0228442 -0.1129475  0.1174113  0.000973987

Missing waves are handled by full-information maximum likelihood. LCGA is nested in the GMM with the same number of classes only at the boundary of the parameter space (variances fixed at zero), so the chi-square difference test is not appropriate for that comparison; compare them with information criteria.

Class enumeration works as for latent class models:

fits <- lapply(1:5, function(k) growth(depression, dep1:dep5, K = k, model = "gmm", degree = 2))
lm_table(fits)   # BIC is lowest for four classes

Model fit ─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────── Model K Par. LL AIC BIC saBIC Entropy Smallest (%) ─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────── Model 1 1 14 -7305.024 14638.048 14699.605 14655.159 — — Model 2 2 18 -7200.172 14436.344 14515.489 14458.344 0.918 20.7 Model 3 3 22 -7191.470 14426.940 14523.673 14453.829 0.874 9.4 Model 4 4 26 -7168.432 14388.864 14503.184 14420.641 0.795 9.5 Model 5 5 30 -7163.026 14386.051 14517.959 14422.717 0.814 1.0 ─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────── LL = log-likelihood; Par. = free parameters; saBIC = sample-size adjusted BIC; Smallest = smallest class (estimated proportion).

Parallel processes: depression and anxiety

A parallel-process model fits the trajectories of several outcomes jointly: each class has a trajectory for every outcome, and with "gmm" the growth factors of all outcomes are correlated within class. depression also has anxiety symptoms (GAD-7, anx1–anx5), generated with class-specific trajectories and growth factors correlated with those of depression.

pp <- depression |> growth(processes = list(dep1:dep5, anx1:anx5), K = 4, model = "gmm")
convergence(pp)
#> Convergence check: ✓ no problems found
#>   best start converged      yes (69 EM iterations)
#>   stage-2 starts converged  20 / 20
#>   best LL replicated        19 times
#>   LL at EM / after Newton   -13331.8338 / -13331.8338 (gain 0.0e+00; max |gradient| 8.0e-11)
#>   smallest class            0.087
#>   · EM converged; 1 Newton steps (polish = true) raised the log-likelihood by 5.1e-11 (max |gradient| 2.8e-04 → 2.0e-10); the reported solution is the Newton one
pp

round(growthparams(pp)$psi, 2)   # joint covariance of the growth factors of both outcomes
#>                dep1:intercept dep1:linear anx1:intercept anx1:linear
#> dep1:intercept           2.95       -0.26           0.92       -0.14
#> dep1:linear             -0.26        0.34          -0.09        0.14
#> anx1:intercept           0.92       -0.09           2.66       -0.18
#> anx1:linear             -0.14        0.14          -0.18        0.17

times and degree can be given per process, for example degree = c(2, 1) (quadratic depression, linear anxiety; slower, about half a minute here).

Covariates, weights, classify(), r3step(), bch() and dcat() work for growth models as for latent class models (see vignette("auxiliary")).

References

Collins, L. M., & Lanza, S. T. (2010). Latent Class and Latent Transition Analysis. Wiley.

Muthén, B., & Shedden, K. (1999). Finite mixture modeling with mixture outcomes using the EM algorithm. Biometrics, 55(2), 463–469.

Nagin, D. S. (1999). Analyzing developmental trajectories: A semiparametric, group-based approach. Psychological Methods, 4(2), 139–157.
